toranaga-ieyasu.title: Toranaga is Tokugawa Ieyasu
toranaga-ieyasu.summary: The Shōgun hero is based on the man who unified Japan. Find armour from his era in the museum.
detail: Lord Toranaga in Shōgun is modelled on Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616). Other matches: Blackthorne = William Adams, Ishido = Ishida Mitsunari, Mariko ≈ Hosokawa Gracia, the Taikō = Toyotomi Hideyoshi.
Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and became shogun in 1603. His family ruled Japan from Edo (today's Tokyo) until 1868.
The museum stands on land of Kan'ei-ji, the Tokugawa family temple, built in 1625 to guard the north-east of Edo Castle, the direction believed to let in evil.
toranaga-ieyasu.check: Tokyo National Museum, Honkan rooms 5–6 (2nd floor): look for armour from the late 1500s and early 1600s (Momoyama and early Edo periods). Displays rotate, so a piece owned by Ieyasu himself may not be out.

sekigahara.title: Sekigahara, 1600
sekigahara.summary: One battle decided who ruled Japan for the next ~250 years.
detail: On 21 October 1600, about 160,000 samurai met at Sekigahara, a valley in today's Gifu Prefecture: Ieyasu's Eastern Army against the Western Army led by Ishida Mitsunari (Ishido in Shōgun).
The battle turned in a few hours when Kobayakawa Hideaki switched sides and attacked the Western Army.
Ieyasu became shogun in 1603. The Tokugawa shogunate lasted until the Meiji Restoration of 1868, about 265 years of peace known as the Edo period.
After the battle Ieyasu rewarded his allies with land: Himeji went to his son-in-law Ikeda Terumasa, who built the castle we see on Sat 14.
sekigahara.check: Linked across the trip: the museum armour (Wed 11), Himeji Castle (Sat 14), Nijō Castle (Sun 15) and Osaka Castle (Sat 21).

matcha-bowl.title: Turn the bowl before you drink
matcha-bowl.summary: In a tea ceremony you turn the matcha bowl so you don't drink from its front.
detail: Every tea bowl has a 'front' (shōmen): its most beautiful side, which the host turns towards the guest.
Out of modesty the guest turns the bowl about a quarter, usually clockwise twice, so as not to drink from the front, then turns it back before returning it.
Usucha (thin tea) is frothy and served one bowl per guest; koicha (thick tea) is kneaded and shared from one bowl.
Matcha is ground tencha: the bushes are shaded for ~3 weeks before harvest, and a stone mill grinds only ~40 g an hour.
matcha-bowl.check: At Nakajima no Ochaya (Thu 12) and at the Taihō-an tea ceremony in Uji (Wed 18).

chasen-takayama.title: The whisk comes from one village
chasen-takayama.summary: Over 90% of Japan's bamboo tea whisks are made in Takayama, Ikoma (Nara).
detail: The chasen is carved from a single piece of bamboo, split into up to 100 or more fine tines.
Takayama in Ikoma city has made whisks for about 500 years; the craft is passed down in a few families.
Look at the whisk you get with your matcha and count the tines.
chasen-takayama.check: At the teahouse in Hamarikyū (Thu 12) and Taihō-an (Wed 18).

vending-machines.title: Count the vending machines
vending-machines.summary: Japan has fewer drink machines than ever, and still about 1.95 million.
detail: In 2025 Japan had about 1.95 million soft-drink vending machines, the first time below 2 million since 1994.
The peak was about 2.47 million in 2014; rising prices and convenience stores have cut the number since.
That is still roughly one drink machine for every 60 people. Many sell hot drinks in winter: look for the red 'あたたかい' (warm) labels.
vending-machines.check: Count them on the walk to Takao's cable car or around Shinjuku (Fri 13). Try a hot can.

adams-anjin.title: Anjin: the Englishman who became a samurai
adams-anjin.summary: William Adams, the real Blackthorne, lived in Tokyo; 'anjin' means pilot.
detail: William Adams reached Japan in 1600 as pilot of the Dutch ship Liefde, the first Englishman in Japan.
Ieyasu made him an adviser and a samurai with the name Miura Anjin: 'anjin' means pilot or navigator.
His Edo house stood in today's Nihonbashi Muromachi; the street was called Anjin-chō, marked by a small plaque.
He met Ieyasu first in Osaka in 1600 (Osaka Castle, Sat 21).
adams-anjin.check: Anjin-chō plaque next to Mitsukoshi Nihombashi (Fri 13, Option B).

himeji-terumasa.title: Himeji was a reward for Sekigahara
himeji-terumasa.summary: Ieyasu gave Himeji to his son-in-law, who built the keep you climb today.
detail: Ikeda Terumasa fought for Ieyasu at Sekigahara (1600) and was married to Ieyasu's daughter Tokuhime. As a reward he received the Harima domain, worth about 520,000 koku of rice.
He rebuilt Hideyoshi's smaller castle into the present complex between 1601 and 1609. The keep was meant to watch the western daimyō, many of whom had fought against Ieyasu.
Later Ieyasu's granddaughter Senhime, widow of Hideyori (Hideyoshi's son), married into the Honda family and lived in the Nishi-no-maru; the Hyakken corridor was her household's wing.
himeji-terumasa.check: In the Nishi-no-maru corridor, look for the panels on Senhime. In the keep, find the two great central pillars (east and west).

himeji-okiku.title: The ghost in Okiku's Well
himeji-okiku.summary: A maid accused of losing a precious plate haunts a well inside the castle.
detail: In the Banshū Sarayashiki story, the servant Okiku is falsely accused of losing one of ten treasured plates and thrown into a well.
Each night her ghost counts the plates: 'one, two… nine', and screams at the missing tenth.
The well in the castle grounds is linked to the story. It is one of Japan's most famous ghost tales and inspired many later stories.
himeji-okiku.check: Find Okiku's Well (Okiku-ido) near the Bizen-maru on the way to the keep; the guide usually stops there.

nightingale-floors.title: Floors that sing to warn of intruders
nightingale-floors.summary: Nijō's corridors chirp under every step, so nobody can sneak up on the shogun.
detail: The 'uguisu-bari' floors chirp like a Japanese bush warbler (uguisu) when you walk on them.
Iron clamps under the boards rub against the nails as the boards move, making the sound.
It is often told as an anti-ninja alarm. Some historians think the sound may first have come from wear, then been kept and celebrated.
nightingale-floors.check: In the Ninomaru Palace corridor, try to walk silently: it is almost impossible.

kodaiji-ieyasu.title: Ieyasu paid for his rival's widow's temple
kodaiji-ieyasu.summary: Kōdai-ji honours Hideyoshi, but much of it was paid for by the man who took his place.
detail: Nene (Kita no Mandokoro) founded Kōdai-ji in 1606 to pray for Hideyoshi.
Tokugawa Ieyasu funded much of the building. Keeping Hideyoshi's respected widow friendly helped him win over the Toyotomi loyalists before he finished them off at Osaka in 1615.
Nene lived nearby for the rest of her life and is buried in the Otamaya with Hideyoshi.
kodaiji-ieyasu.check: In the Otamaya, look for the gold makie lacquer and the wooden figures of Hideyoshi and Nene.

kiyomizu-jump.title: Jumping off the stage of Kiyomizu
kiyomizu-jump.summary: The saying means 'to take the plunge', and people really did jump.
detail: 'Kiyomizu no butai kara tobioriru' means to make a bold decision, like jumping off the stage.

In the Edo period people jumped believing Kannon would grant their wish if they survived. Temple records list 234 jumps between 1694 and 1864, and about 85% survived (trees and soft soil broke the fall).
Jumping was banned in 1872.
kiyomizu-jump.check: From the stage, look down: it is about 13 m to the slope. From Okuno-in, count the pillars under the stage.

sannenzaka.title: Three years of bad luck on Sannenzaka
sannenzaka.summary: Fall on the 'three-year slope' and, the legend says, you die within three years.
detail: The superstition says a fall on Sannenzaka brings death (or bad luck) within three years.
The cure: buy a hollow gourd (hyōtan) at the shop at the bottom of the steps. Gourds are believed to absorb bad luck.
The legend may be a way to keep pilgrims careful on the steep, often wet steps to Kiyomizu.
sannenzaka.check: Find the gourd shop at the bottom of the Sannenzaka steps.

maiko-collar.title: Red collar for maiko, white for geiko
maiko-collar.summary: The collar colour tells you who is an apprentice and who is a full geiko.
detail: Maiko (apprentices, usually 15–20) wear a red collar, long hanging obi (darari obi), tall okobo clogs and their own hair in elaborate styles.
When a maiko becomes a geiko, she 'turns her collar' (erikae) from red to white.
Geiko wear a shorter obi, lower zōri and usually a wig. They are the senior, fully trained artists.
maiko-collar.check: If you see one at dusk, look at the collar and the obi (no photos without asking).

eisai-tea.title: The monk who brought tea back
eisai-tea.summary: Kennin-ji's founder brought tea seeds from China and wrote Japan's first book on tea.
detail: Eisai (1141–1215) studied Zen in China and brought back tea seeds in 1191.
In 1211 he wrote the Kissa Yōjōki ('Drinking tea for health'), calling tea a medicine.
Every year on 20 April Kennin-ji holds a tea ceremony in his memory (Yotsugashira chakai).
eisai-tea.check: At Kennin-ji, look for the small tea garden near the Hōjō, planted in Eisai's honour.

ginkakuji-silver.title: The Silver Pavilion has no silver
ginkakuji-silver.summary: Ginkaku-ji was never covered in silver, and probably never meant to be.
detail: The name 'Ginkaku' became common only in the Edo period, as a contrast to Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion built by Yoshimasa's grandfather.
A 2007 study of the building found no silver leaf, only traces of black lacquer.
Moonlight on the lacquer and on the raked sand may have given the 'silver' look.
ginkakuji-silver.check: Look at the pavilion's dark wood. Then the sand cone (Kōgetsudai): it is said to reflect moonlight.

sanjusangendo-arrows.title: 8,133 arrows in 24 hours
sanjusangendo-arrows.summary: Archers once shot the full length of Sanjūsangen-dō's veranda all day and night.
detail: In the Edo period samurai competed in the Tōshiya: shooting arrows along the 120 m west veranda without hitting the roof or pillars.
In 1686 Wasa Daihachirō shot 13,053 arrows in 24 hours, and 8,133 reached the end.
Today the Ōmato taikai is held each January: young archers in kimono shoot at 60 m in the garden.
sanjusangendo-arrows.check: On the west veranda, look up at the roof beams: old arrow marks are still in the wood.

eikan-mikaeri.title: The Buddha who looked back
eikan-mikaeri.summary: Eikan-dō's Amida turns his head over his shoulder; legend says he called to a monk.
detail: In 1082 the monk Eikan was walking around the Amida statue, chanting, at dawn.
The statue stepped down and walked ahead, then looked back and said: 'Eikan, you are slow.'
The statue has kept that pose ever since: the Mikaeri ('looking-back') Amida.
eikan-mikaeri.check: In the Amida-dō, stand to the right of the statue to see its face.

inari-torii.title: 10,000 torii, all paid for
inari-torii.summary: Every torii at Fushimi Inari was donated by a person or company.
detail: About 10,000 torii line the mountain paths. The donor's name and the date are written on the back of each.
A small torii costs a few hundred thousand yen; a large one over a million.
Inari is the god of rice and business, so many donors are companies praying for success.
inari-torii.check: Walk back down: you only see the writing on the uphill side of each torii.

byodoin-coin.title: Byōdō-in is in your wallet
byodoin-coin.summary: The Phoenix Hall is on the 10-yen coin.
detail: The Phoenix Hall (1053) is on the back of the 10-yen coin.
Its bronze phoenix was on the old 10,000-yen note (2004 series).
The hall was built to show Amida's Western Paradise on earth, at a time when people believed the age of the Buddha's law was ending (1052).
byodoin-coin.check: Hold a 10-yen coin up in front of the hall and compare.

wooden-halls.title: Japan's two biggest wooden halls in one day
wooden-halls.summary: Zaō-dō in the morning, the Great Buddha Hall in the afternoon: compare them.
detail: Kinpusen-ji's Zaō-dō (rebuilt 1592) is about 34 m tall and is usually called the second-largest wooden building in Japan.
Tōdai-ji's Daibutsuden (rebuilt 1709) is about 49 m tall and 57 m wide. The original hall from the 8th century was even wider, about 86 m.
Both halls house giant figures: the 7 m blue Zaō Gongen and the 15 m bronze Buddha.
wooden-halls.check: Count the pillars across the front of each hall, and look at the roofs: cypress bark at Zaō-dō, tiles at Tōdai-ji.

hideyoshi-hanami.title: Hideyoshi's 5,000-guest picnic
hideyoshi-hanami.summary: In 1594 Hideyoshi brought about 5,000 people to Yoshino for a five-day cherry party.
detail: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, then ruler of Japan, held the great Yoshino flower-viewing in spring 1594, with daimyō including Tokugawa Ieyasu, poets and tea masters.
It rained for three days; legend says Hideyoshi threatened to burn the mountain if the rain did not stop, and the next day was clear.
He used Yoshimizu Shrine (then a temple) as his headquarters.
hideyoshi-hanami.check: In Yoshimizu Shrine's Shoin, look for objects from Hideyoshi's visit.

yoshitsune-yoshino.title: Yoshitsune's hiding place
yoshitsune-yoshino.summary: The tragic samurai hero hid at Yoshimizu with his lover Shizuka and the giant monk Benkei.
detail: Minamoto no Yoshitsune won the Genpei War (1185) for his brother Yoritomo, who then turned against him.
Hunted, he hid in Yoshino in 1185 with Shizuka Gozen and Benkei before escaping north. Shizuka was captured in the snow on the mountain.
The kabuki play 'Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura' ('Yoshitsune and the Thousand Cherry Trees') is set here.
yoshitsune-yoshino.check: In the Shoin, find the small room called 'Yoshitsune's hiding room' and Benkei's armour display.

kofukuji-ashura.title: The three-faced Ashura
kofukuji-ashura.summary: Nara's most loved statue is a former demon turned guardian, made of dry lacquer in 734.
detail: Ashura was a fighting demon in Indian myth who became a protector of Buddhism.
Kōfuku-ji's statue has three faces and six thin arms and the face of a serious boy; it is hollow dry lacquer and weighs only about 15 kg.
It survived several fires because monks could carry it out.
kofukuji-ashura.check: In the National Treasure Museum, compare the expressions on the three faces.

nara-deer.title: Deer that bow
nara-deer.summary: Nara's deer bow for crackers, and are protected as a Natural Monument.
detail: The deer are sacred messengers of Kasuga Taisha's god, who is said to have arrived riding a white deer.
Until 1637 killing one could be punished by death.
They learned to bow because people bow to them before giving shika senbei.
nara-deer.check: Bow to a deer holding a cracker and see if it bows back.

daibutsu-nostril.title: Squeeze through the Buddha's nostril
daibutsu-nostril.summary: A pillar in the Great Buddha Hall has a hole as big as the Buddha's nostril.
detail: The hole at the base of a pillar behind the Buddha is about 30 by 37 cm, said to match one nostril.
Crawling through is believed to bring enlightenment in your next life (or good luck).
Children go through easily; adults sometimes get stuck.
daibutsu-nostril.check: Find the pillar behind and to the right of the Buddha (north-east), usually with a queue.

omizutori.title: A ceremony never missed since 752
omizutori.summary: Nigatsu-dō's fire ritual has been held every year for over 1,270 years.
detail: Shuni-e (Omizutori) runs for two weeks every March; monks run along the balcony with burning torches.
It has been held every year since 752, even during wars and the 1667 fire that destroyed the hall.
'Omizutori' means 'drawing sacred water' from the Wakasa well below the hall.
omizutori.check: On the balcony, look for the soot marks on the wood and the iron lanterns.

migawari-zaru.title: Red monkeys that take your bad luck
migawari-zaru.summary: Naramachi houses hang red cloth monkeys that take misfortune in your place.
detail: Migawari-zaru ('substitute monkeys') are red stuffed monkeys with their hands and feet tied, hung under the eaves.
They are linked to the Kōshin faith: the monkey takes illness and bad luck instead of the family.
People write a wish on the back, and must give up one desire for it to work.
migawari-zaru.check: Count the monkeys on a street and find the Kōshin-dō hall that sells them.

no-double-dip.title: One dip only
no-double-dip.summary: In Shinsekai the kushikatsu sauce is shared, so dipping a bitten skewer twice is the one big sin.
detail: Each table has a steel pot of thin sauce shared by everyone; signs say 二度づけ禁止 ('no second dipping').
If you need more sauce, scoop it with the free raw cabbage leaves and drip it on.
Kushikatsu began in Shinsekai in 1929 as cheap fried food for labourers.
no-double-dip.check: Find the 二度づけ禁止 sign at your table, and use the cabbage trick.

godairiki-stones.title: Find the three lucky stones
godairiki-stones.summary: At Sumiyoshi Taisha people search a gravel plot for small stones marked 五, 大 and 力.
detail: Gosho-gozen is the spot where the shrine's gods are said to have first appeared; it is fenced and full of pebbles.
Finding three stones written 五 (five), 大 (great) and 力 (power) brings luck: the 'five great powers' of long life, wealth, wisdom, happiness and health.
When your wish comes true, you return the stones with three more of your own.
godairiki-stones.check: Behind the first main hall: look for the small fenced gravel plot with a sign 五所御前.

kongo-gumi.title: The world's oldest company built this temple
kongo-gumi.summary: Kongō Gumi was founded in 578 to build Shitennō-ji and ran for over 1,400 years.
detail: Prince Shōtoku brought carpenters from the Korean kingdom of Baekje to build Shitennō-ji; one of them founded Kongō Gumi in 578.
The family firm kept building and repairing temples for 40 generations.
It ran into debt in the 2000s and became part of a larger builder in 2006, but still works on Shitennō-ji under its old name.
kongo-gumi.check: In the central precinct, note the straight line of gate, pagoda, main hall and lecture hall: the oldest temple layout in Japan.

gracia-mariko.title: Mariko was a real woman
gracia-mariko.summary: Shōgun's Lady Mariko is based on Hosokawa Gracia, who died in Osaka in 1600.
detail: Tama was a daughter of Akechi Mitsuhide, the general who betrayed Oda Nobunaga in 1582.
She converted to Christianity and was baptised Gracia.
In 1600 Ishida Mitsunari tried to take daimyō wives as hostages; she refused, had her retainer kill her and the mansion burned. Her death turned many daimyō against Ishida, months before Sekigahara.
gracia-mariko.check: At Osaka Cathedral (Tamatsukuri), find her statue and read the plaque; the cathedral stands on the Hosokawa mansion site.

kitsune-udon.title: Udon for foxes
kitsune-udon.summary: Kitsune udon was invented in Osaka in 1893 at Matsubaya.
detail: The owner started serving the sweet fried tofu (inari-age) from sushi on top of udon.
Kitsune means fox: foxes, messengers of Inari, are said to love fried tofu.
In Osaka you ask for 'kitsune'; in Kyoto the same name can mean something different.
kitsune-udon.check: At Usami-tei Matsubaya, look for the framed history on the wall.

escalator-sides.title: Osaka stands on the right
escalator-sides.summary: Tokyo stands on the left of escalators; Osaka on the right.
detail: The most common story: before the 1970 Osaka Expo, Hankyu railway asked passengers to stand right, following the international habit.
Tokyo kept the left, so the country has two rules.
Kyoto stations are mixed, depending on how many visitors use them.
escalator-sides.check: Compare on the Midōsuji Line in Osaka with what you saw in Tokyo.

number-551.title: Why 551?
number-551.summary: The name of Osaka's pork-bun chain comes from its old phone number.
detail: The first shop's phone number ended in 551.
Read 'go-go-ichi', it also sounds like 'koko ga ichiban': 'this is the best'.
An old TV advert made the line '551 ga aru toki' ('when there's 551') famous across Kansai.
number-551.check: Look at the red 551 logo on the box.

winged-gyoza.title: Gyoza with wings
winged-gyoza.summary: Kamata's winged gyoza were invented in 1983 by a cook from Dalian.
detail: Yagi Isao, born in Dalian, opened Nihao in Kamata in 1983.
He adapted Shanghai's pan-fried buns: a thin flour-and-water batter poured in the pan forms a crisp 'wing' joining the dumplings.
Kamata now has several 'winged gyoza' houses run by his family and former staff.
winged-gyoza.check: Lift the plate: the wing should come up as one sheet.

edo-era.title: The Edo period in five minutes
edo-era.summary: For 265 years the shoguns kept Japan at peace, closed and busy.
detail: From 1603 to 1868 the Tokugawa shoguns ruled from Edo, today's Tokyo. By the 1700s it had about a million people, among the largest cities in the world.
Sakoku, the closed-country policy of the 1630s, limited foreign trade mainly to the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki.
Under sankin-kōtai, each daimyō had to live in Edo every other year and leave his family there. The costly processions kept lords poor and loyal, and fed the roads and inns.
Peace and rich townspeople produced ukiyo-e prints, kabuki, professional sumo and Edo-mae sushi, once a fast food.
edo-era.check: At the museum, look for ukiyo-e and for screens showing daimyō processions. In Yanaka, picture the temple town that grew around Edo.

shinto-buddhism.title: Born Shintō, buried Buddhist
shinto-buddhism.summary: Most Japanese use both religions, for different moments of life.
detail: Shintō is the native worship of kami, spirits of places and forces. Buddhism arrived from Korea in the 6th century.
Traditionally, births and weddings go to the shrine and funerals to the temple.
For about 1,000 years the two were mixed in the same sites. A government order of 1868 forced them apart (shinbutsu bunri), and many temple treasures were destroyed.
shinto-buddhism.check: Each stop: torii and straw rope = shrine; big gate with guardians and incense = temple. See if you can tell before reading the sign.

purity-water.title: Why everyone washes first
purity-water.summary: Hand-washing, shoes off and hot baths share one idea: purity.
detail: Kegare is ritual pollution, and misogi is cleansing with water. In myth, the god Izanagi washes in a river after visiting the land of the dead.
The basin at a shrine is a small misogi. So, loosely, are taking off shoes and washing before getting into a bath.
Salt has the same job: sumo wrestlers throw it on the ring, and some restaurants put small cones of it by the door (morijio).
purity-water.check: Look for small white cones of salt at restaurant entrances, mostly in the evening.

omotenashi.title: Why nobody wants your tip
omotenashi.summary: Omotenashi means service given without expecting anything back.
detail: Good service is simply part of the job, so a tip can embarrass staff. Some will chase you down the street to return it.
Payment goes on the small tray at the till, not hand to hand.
The word is linked to the tea ceremony, where the host anticipates what a guest needs before it is asked.
omotenashi.check: Watch for the tray by the till. On the Shinkansen, watch the cleaning crew and conductors bow to the carriage.

omiyage.title: Gifts in individual wrappers
omiyage.summary: Omiyage are souvenirs owed to colleagues and family, and every region has its own.
detail: The custom is often traced to pilgrims bringing back blessed items from shrines to those who stayed home.
Boxes are made to share: each sweet is wrapped separately and the count is printed on the box.
Furoshiki are the square cloths used to wrap and carry gifts. They were named after bathhouses, where they held clothes.
omiyage.check: At Tokyo or Kyoto Station, find a sweet sold only in that region (for Kyoto, yatsuhashi).

shichi-go-san.title: Children in kimono on Sun 15 Nov
shichi-go-san.summary: Shichi-Go-San (7-5-3) falls on the exact day we are in Kyoto.
detail: On 15 November, children aged 3, 5 and 7 visit shrines dressed in kimono to give thanks and pray for health. Many families choose a nearby weekend.
Each child gets chitose-ame, "thousand-year candy": long, thin sticks of red and white in a printed bag, for a long life.
The ages come from old rites: first letting the hair grow, first hakama for boys, first adult obi for girls.
shichi-go-san.check: Near any shrine on Sun 15, look for tiny kimono and the long candy bags. Ask before photographing children.

momijigari.title: Hunting the red leaves
momijigari.summary: Momijigari, "maple hunting", became a popular outing in the Edo period.
detail: Nobles had long gone to admire autumn leaves. In the Edo period, townspeople joined in.
"Hunting" is used for a harmless pleasure, as with mushroom or strawberry picking.
Maples turn from the mountains downward. Our mid-November dates are early colour in Kyoto, with higher ground ahead of the city.
momijigari.check: Compare the leaf colour at Takao (Fri 13), Arashiyama (Sun 15) and Yoshino (Wed 18).

kinro-kansha.title: A harvest rite on our last day
kinro-kansha.summary: Labour Thanksgiving Day, Mon 23 Nov, is a public holiday with very old roots.
detail: Kinrō Kansha no Hi became a holiday in 1948, replacing Niiname-sai.
At Niiname-sai the emperor offers the year's new rice to the gods and tastes it himself. It is still held at the palace on the night of 23 November.
Traditionally, people did not eat the new rice until this rite was done.
kinro-kansha.check: At Haneda, look for holiday notices and Japanese flags.

tori-no-ichi.title: The rake fair we just miss
tori-no-ichi.summary: Tori-no-ichi fills Asakusa with lucky rakes, on 7 and 19 Nov in 2026.
detail: The fair is held on the "rooster days" of November, which come round every 12 days. In 2026 they fall on Sat 7 and Thu 19, so it misses our Tokyo stay.
Stalls at Ōtori Shrine, in the Asakusa area, sell kumade: decorated bamboo rakes to "rake in" good fortune.
When a rake sells, the stall and buyer clap in rhythm together. Businesses buy a bigger one every year.
tori-no-ichi.check: Look for kumade on the walls of restaurants and shops around Asakusa.

yukata-left.title: Left over right, always
yukata-left.summary: Wrap a yukata the wrong way and you are dressed as a corpse.
detail: Everyone, men and women, wraps the left side over the right. The right over left is for dressing the dead.
A law of 719 is said to have fixed the rule across the country.
A quick test: you should be able to slip your right hand into the fold at your chest.
yukata-left.check: At Chikurinin (Wed 18), check each other before going to dinner.

shugendo.title: The mountain monks of Yoshino
shugendo.summary: Yoshino is the home of Shugendō, part Buddhism, part mountain worship.
detail: Its founder, the 7th-century ascetic En no Gyōja, is said to have had a vision of the fierce Zaō Gongen on Mt Ōmine.
He is said to have carved the image from cherry wood, which is why cherry trees are sacred here and were planted by pilgrims. Today there are about 30,000.
Yamabushi monks still walk the 1,000-year-old Ōmine route. Its peak, Sanjōgatake, remains closed to women.
shugendo.check: At Zaō-dō, look for the conch shells and yamabushi gear. Listen for a horn.

itadakimasu.title: What itadakimasu really says
itadakimasu.summary: It is not "bon appétit". It means "I humbly receive".
detail: Itadaku is the humble verb for receiving, and is linked to raising something above your head (itadaki also means a summit).
The thanks go to everyone who made the food, and to the plants and animals themselves.
Gochisōsama, said after eating, is written with characters for running around: thanks for the effort of gathering a feast.
itadakimasu.check: Say it with hands together at the next meal, and listen for it at the tables around you.

sumo-shinto.title: Sumo is a Shintō rite
sumo-shinto.summary: The ring is sacred ground, and the top champion wears a shrine rope.
detail: The clay ring (dohyō) is consecrated before each tournament, and a roof hangs above it like a shrine's.
Wrestlers throw salt to purify it. A yokozuna wears a thick white rope with zigzag paper, the same as the shimenawa on sacred places.
Ryōgoku is Tokyo's sumo district, with the Kokugikan and many stables. Chanko-nabe is what wrestlers eat to gain weight.
This month's tournament runs 8–22 Nov in Fukuoka, not Tokyo.
sumo-shinto.check: At dinner in Ryōgoku, see whether the TV has the Fukuoka bouts on, usually late afternoon. Look for wrestlers in yukata.

new-year.title: 108 strokes of the bell
new-year.summary: New Year is Japan's biggest holiday, and it all happens at temples and shrines.
detail: On New Year's Eve, temple bells ring 108 times (joya-no-kane), once for each human desire or passion.
Hatsumōde is the first shrine visit of the year. The busiest sites draw millions in three days.
Kadomatsu pine-and-bamboo pairs stand at doors to welcome the god of the year. Osechi food comes in layered boxes, each item a pun for good luck.
new-year.check: Find a big temple bell and see how the log striker hangs.

power-split.title: A country with two electricities
power-split.summary: Tokyo runs at 50 Hz, Osaka at 60 Hz, because of a choice made in the 1890s.
detail: Tokyo bought generators from Germany (50 Hz), and Osaka bought them from America (60 Hz).
The split runs roughly along the Fuji River and has never been unified. Special converter stations link the two halves.
Our Nozomi crosses the line on Sat 14 without you noticing.
power-split.check: Look at Mt Fuji from the Nozomi on Sat 14: you are close to the line between the two systems.

kansai-kanto.title: Kansai and Kantō are different countries
kansai-kanto.summary: Broth, jokes, words and even escalators change between Tokyo and Osaka.
detail: Kantō is the Tokyo region, Kansai the area around Osaka, Kyoto and Nara.
Kansai udon broth is pale, from kombu and light soy. Tokyo broth is dark.
Thank you in Osaka can be ōkini, and "no good" is akan rather than dame.
kansai-kanto.check: Compare the colour of a soup in Tokyo with one in Osaka. Listen for ōkini in a market.

train-punctual.title: Delays in seconds
train-punctual.summary: The Tōkaidō Shinkansen averaged a 1.4-minute delay per train in FY2024, weather included.
detail: JR Central reports 1.4 minutes per train for FY2024, counting delays from natural disasters. Its figure for FY2016 was 24 seconds.
In 2017 the Tsukuba Express apologised for leaving 20 seconds early. In 2018 JR West did the same for 25 seconds.
Drivers and staff use shisa-kanko, "pointing and calling": they point at signals and say what they see aloud, to cut errors.
train-punctual.check: On Nozomi 111 (Sat 14), compare your watch with 06:06 and 09:00. On platforms, watch the staff point and call.

osaka-tokyo.title: Osaka vs Tokyo
osaka-tokyo.summary: Tokyo dresses up, Osaka eats and answers back.
detail: An old saying contrasts Kyoto, where people ruin themselves on clothes, with Osaka, where they ruin themselves on food (kuidaore).
In the Edo period, Osaka was "the nation's kitchen", where rice from every domain was traded.
Osaka is the home of manzai comedy. The joke goes that if you point a finger and say "bang", an Osakan will play dead.
osaka-tokyo.check: Do the people in the Osaka queue stand closer and talk more than in Tokyo?

kinkaku-fire.title: The monk who burned the Golden Pavilion
kinkaku-fire.summary: Kinkaku-ji is a 1955 copy of a building destroyed by a novice.
detail: In 1950 a 21-year-old monk set fire to the 14th-century pavilion. Yukio Mishima turned the story into a novel in 1956.
It was rebuilt in 1955, with more gold than the original is thought to have had.
It is not on our route. Its sister building is the Silver Pavilion, built by the grandson of its founder.
kinkaku-fire.check: At Ginkaku-ji, imagine it covered in gold, as its name might suggest.

five-hanamachi.title: Kyoto's five geisha districts
five-hanamachi.summary: Gion is the famous one, but Kamishichiken is the oldest.
detail: Kyoto has five hanamachi: Gion Kōbu, Miyagawachō, Pontochō, Kamishichiken and Gion Higashi.
Kamishichiken grew up with seven teahouses built from timber left over from rebuilding Kitano Tenmangū in the 15th century.
Each district has its own crest, printed on the lanterns outside its teahouses.
five-hanamachi.check: Look at the lanterns: the crest of Gion Kōbu is a ring of linked dumplings. Pontochō's is a plover.

ichigen-san.title: No first-time guests
ichigen-san.summary: Ichigen-san okotowari: without an introduction, the door stays shut.
detail: Ochaya teahouses admit only guests introduced by a regular.
The teahouse carries the bill, arranges the geiko, and can call a taxi or a doctor. So it relies on trust built over years.
Ichiriki-tei, over 300 years old, appears in the story of the 47 rōnin: their leader Ōishi drank there to fool his enemies.
ichigen-san.check: Find Ichiriki-tei's red walls at the corner of Shijō and Hanamikoji.

edo-castle.title: A castle with no keep
edo-castle.summary: Edo Castle lost its tower in 1657, and nobody rebuilt it.
detail: The Great Fire of Meireki burned most of Edo and the castle's tower, the tallest ever built in Japan.
The stone base was remade, but the money went to rebuilding the city instead.
Today the Imperial Palace stands on the site. The Edo-Tokyo Museum was built to match the old keep's height.
edo-castle.check: From the Palace side of Tokyo Station, look for the moats and the massive stone walls.

ikebana-rokkakudo.title: Flower arranging began beside a pond
ikebana-rokkakudo.summary: Ikenobo, the oldest ikebana school, started at Rokkakudō in Kyoto.
detail: Monks at Rokkakudō offered flowers to the Buddha. The priest's hut by the pond gave the school its name.
Ikenobo's oldest records date from the 1460s. Rokkakudō also has a "navel stone", said to mark the centre of old Kyoto.
In 1927 Sogetsu broke the rules with a modern approach. Its Tokyo headquarters has a stone garden by Isamu Noguchi.
ikebana-rokkakudo.check: In hotels and restaurants, look for an arrangement with three main lines: heaven, earth and human.

bonsai-stories.title: Bonsai older than the shoguns
bonsai-stories.summary: One tree has survived 500 years of care, another the atomic bomb.
detail: The Imperial collection has a pine of over 500 years, Sandai-Shōgun no Matsu, said to have been tended by the third Tokugawa shogun, Iemitsu.
Omiya Bonsai Village began after the 1923 earthquake, when Tokyo growers moved north for clean air and space.
A pine trained since 1625 survived the Hiroshima bomb inside a walled nursery. It was given to the US in 1976, and its story only came out in 2001.
bonsai-stories.check: Look for bonsai outside old houses in Yanaka.

rikyu-gold.title: Two-mat hut vs golden room
rikyu-gold.summary: Rikyū perfected plain tea, and served a ruler who loved gold.
detail: Sen no Rikyū (1522–1591) taught wabi: rough bowls, tiny rooms, nothing to spare. His only surviving tea room, Tai-an, has just two mats.
His patron Hideyoshi, the Taikō in Shōgun, had a portable tea room covered in gold.
In 1591 Hideyoshi ordered him to commit seppuku; the reason is still debated.
His great-grandsons founded the three Senke schools: Omotesenke, Urasenke and Mushakōjisenke.
rikyu-gold.check: At Taihō-an, notice how bare the room is, then think of it in gold.

tsuen-1160.title: A tea shop older than the samurai government
tsuen-1160.summary: Tsūen, at Uji Bridge, claims to have been open since 1160.
detail: The family says it served tea to travellers crossing the bridge, and was linked to the guard of the bridge.
It would be one of the oldest shops in the world.
Uji is also the setting for the last ten chapters of The Tale of Genji, the 11th-century novel.
tsuen-1160.check: Find the old wooden shop front at the east end of Uji Bridge, and the Murasaki Shikibu statue nearby.

matcha-shortage.title: The matcha shortage
matcha-shortage.summary: Since 2024, global demand has made shops ration it.
detail: Tencha takes years of work, shaded fields and slow milling, so supply cannot grow quickly.
Big Kyoto names, such as Ippodo and Koyamaen, now commonly limit matcha to about one per person.
Sencha and hōjicha are mostly unlimited, and make a good alternative souvenir.
matcha-shortage.check: Look for the purchase-limit sign at the counter.

hankai-tram.title: Osaka's last streetcar
hankai-tram.summary: The Hankai Tramway is the only street tram left in Osaka Prefecture.
detail: Its Uemachi Line began in 1900 as a horse-drawn railway, and the Hankai Line opened in 1911.
Locals call it Chin-Den, after the sound of its bell.
Some of its cars have been running since 1928.
hankai-tram.check: See if your tram has wooden floors and old fittings. Listen for the "chin".

sumiyoshi-style.title: A shrine with no Buddhist influence
sumiyoshi-style.summary: Sumiyoshi-zukuri is one of the three oldest native shrine styles.
detail: It has straight roofs and no veranda, and it predates the Buddhist architecture that came through China and Korea.
The other old styles are Shinmei at Ise and Taisha at Izumo. The four main halls, last rebuilt in 1810, are National Treasures.
Three of the halls stand in a line facing west, towards the sea, because this was a shrine for sailors.
sumiyoshi-style.check: Compare the roofs here with the curved ones at Shitennō-ji the same day.

otoshi-charge.title: The snack you did not order
otoshi-charge.summary: In an izakaya, the small dish that arrives first is on the bill.
detail: Otōshi is a seat charge in the form of a small appetizer, usually a few hundred yen per person.
It is normal, not a scam, so expect to pay it. Check the menu or ask first if you want to know the price.
Then comes the phrase: toriaezu nama, "a draft beer for now".
otoshi-charge.check: Look for お通し on the receipt.

beer-big-four.title: Four beers rule the taps
beer-big-four.summary: Asahi, Kirin, Sapporo and Suntory dominate, and each bar usually pours just one.
detail: A bar normally has a contract with one brewer, so "nama" means whichever one they pour.
Asahi Super Dry (1987) started the dry-beer boom and changed the Japanese market.
Cheap cans labelled 発泡酒 or 第三のビール are made to pay lower beer tax. Look for them in the konbini.
beer-big-four.check: Spot which brand the glass or the sign shows at each place. Keep a tally through the trip.

kobe-nose.title: Kobe beef has a nose print
kobe-nose.summary: Every certified animal is tracked with a 10-digit number.
detail: Kobe beef comes only from Tajima cattle raised in Hyōgo Prefecture and graded by strict marbling rules.
Each animal has an ID, and nose prints have long been used to identify cattle, like fingerprints.
Certified restaurants display a bronze statue and a certificate naming the animal.
kobe-nose.check: Ask to see the certificate. Look for the 10-digit number.

takoyaki-1935.title: Takoyaki is younger than the Eiffel Tower
takoyaki-1935.summary: Octopus balls were first sold in Osaka in 1935.
detail: Endō Tomekichi of Aizuya developed them from a snack called radio-yaki, filled with beef.
Hearing that Akashi had egg-and-octopus dumplings, he swapped the filling.
The classic Aizuya version has no sauce at all.
takoyaki-1935.check: Watch the cook turn each ball with a pick, a quarter at a time.

sakai-blades.title: From tobacco knives to chefs' knives
sakai-blades.summary: Sakai, just south of Osaka, supplies blades to much of the Japanese kitchen.
detail: Sword and blade making grew in Sakai, and tobacco from the Portuguese in the 16th century created a demand for sharp cutting knives.
The shogunate gave Sakai tobacco knives a seal of quality.
Blades are still divided into specialised crafts: forging, sharpening and handles are often done by different people.
sakai-blades.check: At Kappabashi, ask which shop sells Sakai blades (Jikko does), and how many hands made it.

food-samples.title: Plastic food built a business
food-samples.summary: Kappabashi is the capital of sampuru, realistic models of food.
detail: Wax models appeared in the 1920s. Takizō Iwasaki founded the first major maker in 1932, and is said to have started with an omelette.
Today most are PVC, and a single plate is hand-finished.
Kappabashi's name may come from kappa, water spirits said to have helped dig a canal; a golden kappa stands in the street.
food-samples.check: Find the golden Kappa statue and a shop window of plastic ramen.

ginza-silver.title: Ginza means silver mint
ginza-silver.summary: The shogun's silver coins were once made here.
detail: Ieyasu moved the mint here in 1612: gin is silver, za a guild or seat.
In the 1870s, after a fire, Ginza was rebuilt in brick with Western help, and became the first modern shopping street.
The Wakō clock tower dates from 1932.
ginza-silver.check: Find the Wakō clock at the main Ginza crossing.

senso-ji-statue.title: The statue nobody sees
senso-ji-statue.summary: Sensō-ji was built around a statue that stays hidden.
detail: In 628, says the legend, two fishing brothers pulled a small golden Kannon from the Sumida River.
Whenever they threw it back, it returned. The temple was founded around it.
It is a hibutsu, a hidden image, and is not shown. Tokyo's oldest temple was destroyed in 1945 and rebuilt in concrete.
senso-ji-statue.check: Under the Kaminarimon lantern, look up: a large carved dragon is hidden on its base.

yanaka-survivor.title: The old town that survived
yanaka-survivor.summary: Yanaka came through both the 1923 quake and the 1945 raids.
detail: Much of the area was spared, unlike most of Tokyo, so its temple streets are still pre-war.
Yanaka Cemetery holds Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the last shogun, who gave up power in 1867.
It is also known for its street cats, with cat figures on many rooftops and shops.
yanaka-survivor.check: Count cat figures on Yanaka Ginza, and ask the guide about the last shogun's grave.

tsukiji-toyosu.title: The tuna that cost 333 million yen
tsukiji-toyosu.summary: The inner market moved to Toyosu in 2018; Tsukiji's outer stalls stayed.
detail: The famous wholesale market ran at Tsukiji from 1935 to 2018.
At the first Toyosu New Year auction in 2019, a single bluefin sold for ¥333.6 million.
The buyer was Kiyoshi Kimura, owner of the Sushi Zanmai chain, who has repeatedly paid record prices.
tsukiji-toyosu.check: Look for the Sushi Zanmai branches around Tsukiji and for the tuna-cutting stalls.

hamarikyu-duck.title: The shogun's duck trap
hamarikyu-duck.summary: Hamarikyū was a hunting ground, and its ponds rise and fall with the sea.
detail: The Tokugawa used the garden for falconry and duck hunting, and the trenches for luring ducks still exist.
Its main pond is filled with seawater from Tokyo Bay, so it moves with the tide.
Former US president Ulysses Grant stayed in a house here in 1879, and talked with the Meiji emperor at the garden.
hamarikyu-duck.check: Look for the duck-hunting mounds, and the water gate between the pond and the bay.

takao-tengu.title: Mountain goblins of Takao
takao-tengu.summary: Takao is sacred to tengu, and among the world's most climbed mountains.
detail: Yakuō-in temple, said to date from 744, has statues of long-nosed tengu goblins.
Tengu are mountain spirits, sometimes dangerous, sometimes teachers.
Millions climb every year. Michelin gave it three stars in 2007.
takao-tengu.check: Find the tengu statues and the "octopus cedar" with tangled roots.

himeji-white.title: The castle bombs missed
himeji-white.summary: Himeji survived the 1945 raids, and was once sold for almost nothing.
detail: American bombs burned the city around it in 1945, but the keep was left standing.
In the Meiji era it was sold at auction, and legend says for a few yen. The buyer abandoned it because demolition was too costly.
After the 2009–2015 repairs its plaster was so bright that some joked it was the "White Too Much castle" (shirosugi-jō).
himeji-white.check: Look at the white plaster joints in the roof tiles, a feature designed to resist fire.

nijo-start-end.title: Where the shogunate began and ended
nijo-start-end.summary: Ieyasu celebrated here in 1603, and Yoshinobu gave up power here in 1867.
detail: Ieyasu held his ceremony as shogun at Nijō in 1603.
In 1867, the 15th and last shogun announced in the Ninomaru Palace that he was returning power to the emperor.
So the 265 years of Edo rule start and finish in the same place.
nijo-start-end.check: In the Ōhiroma hall, find the figures that recreate the 1867 scene.

nishiki-jakuchu.title: The painter who saved a market
nishiki-jakuchu.summary: The artist Itō Jakuchū was a Nishiki grocer.
detail: Nishiki has sold food for about 400 years, helped by cold groundwater that kept fish fresh.
Jakuchū, born in 1716 into a grocer family, became a great painter of birds and fish.
In the 1770s he helped keep the market open when officials tried to shut it down.
nishiki-jakuchu.check: Look for art inspired by Jakuchū on the market's shutters and banners.

nanzenji-aqueduct.title: A Roman aqueduct in a Zen temple
nanzenji-aqueduct.summary: A brick water channel runs through Nanzen-ji.
detail: Built in 1890 as part of the Lake Biwa Canal, it brought water and power to a Kyoto that had just lost the capital.
Many people thought it spoiled the temple. Today it is one of the most photographed spots there.
Water still flows along the top.
nanzenji-aqueduct.check: Climb the path to the top and see the running water.

philosopher-path.title: A walk named after a thinker
philosopher-path.summary: Nishida Kitarō is said to have meditated on this canal path.
detail: Nishida (1870–1945), a philosopher at Kyoto University, walked here every day.
The cherry trees along it were planted thanks to the wife of the painter Hashimoto Kansetsu.
The path is about 2 km long.
philosopher-path.check: Find the small stone with Nishida's poem.

shogunzuka.title: The buried clay general
shogunzuka.summary: A statue beneath Shōgunzuka is said to rumble when Kyoto is in danger.
detail: When Emperor Kanmu founded Kyoto in 794, he is said to have buried a clay general in armour on this hill to protect the capital.
Chronicles record that the mound shook before times of disaster.
The Seiryūden platform, on the same hill, is much larger than Kiyomizu's stage.
shogunzuka.check: From the platform, find Kyoto Tower and the line of the old grid.

bamboo-sound.title: Bamboo you are meant to hear
bamboo-sound.summary: The Arashiyama grove is on an official list of sounds worth preserving.
detail: In 1996 Japan's Environment Agency listed 100 "soundscapes", and this grove is one.
Ōkōchi Sansō next door was built by the silent film star Ōkōchi Denjirō, over about 30 years.
Bamboo can grow up to a metre in a day at its peak.

billiken.title: Rub the feet of an American god
billiken.summary: Osaka's lucky Billiken was invented in the United States.
detail: An American art teacher, Florence Pretz, designed the figure in 1908.
It came to Osaka, and a statue was placed in Luna Park, Shinsekai's amusement park, in 1912.
The tower has a figure, and rubbing the soles is said to bring luck.
billiken.check: Find a Billiken in Shinsekai and rub its feet.

glico-man.title: The running man of Dōtonbori
glico-man.summary: The Glico sign has been running since 1935.
detail: Glico sold its caramel as "300 m on one piece". The runner has his arms up at the finish.
The first neon was set up in 1935. The present LED version dates from 2014.
Generations of tourists copy his pose on the bridge.
glico-man.check: Stand on Ebisu Bridge and copy the pose.

mizukake-fudo.title: The statue covered in moss
mizukake-fudo.summary: Hōzen-ji's Fudō is green because everyone splashes water on it.
detail: Visitors pour water over the statue when praying, and the years of water have grown a thick moss.
The temple dates from 1637. It was burned in 1945, but the statue survived.
The alley beside it is a survivor of old Osaka.
mizukake-fudo.check: Take a ladle, splash gently, and look at the shape of the face.

umeda-lift.title: A garden lifted into the sky
umeda-lift.summary: The ring between the Umeda towers was built on the ground, then raised.
detail: The building opened in 1993. The top ring, about 170 m up, was assembled at ground level.
Cables hauled it up between the towers.
Hiroshi Hara, its architect, also designed Kyoto Station.
umeda-lift.check: From the top, look down at the escalators that cross the open air.

osaka-keep-1931.title: The castle with an elevator
osaka-keep-1931.summary: Osaka Castle's keep is a 1931 concrete tower.
detail: Hideyoshi's castle burned in 1615, and a Tokugawa keep was hit by lightning in 1665.
Citizens raised the money for the present tower in 1931, and it survived the war.
Its huge walls, though, are real 1620s Tokugawa work, built by daimyō who were made to compete.
osaka-keep-1931.check: Find the Tako-ishi, the giant "octopus stone" in the walls at the Sakuramon gate.

manhole-art.title: Art under your feet
manhole-art.summary: Japan's manhole covers are designed town by town.
detail: In the 1980s, sewer officials encouraged towns to use local designs, to win public support for the sewers.
Thousands of designs now exist, and there are even collector cards.
Expect castles, flowers, local festivals and cartoon mascots.
manhole-art.check: Photograph one cover in each city, and compare them at the end of the trip.

toilets.title: The toilet control panel
toilets.summary: Japan's heated, washing toilet is a national institution.
detail: TOTO launched its Washlet in 1980. Now most homes have one.
Some public toilets have a "Sound Princess" button that plays running water, to hide noises.
Many station toilets show a map of the stalls by the door.
toilets.check: Find the Otohime button in a public toilet.
